# Before the First Class {.unnumbered}

This page gets your computer ready for the course. Plan on 30 to 45 minutes, most of which is waiting for things to download, and please do it *before* our first meeting, so we can spend class time on statistics and not on installation troubleshooting. Week 1 explains *why* the workflow looks the way it does; this page is just the steps.

## Step 1: Install R

R does the computing. Download it from [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org):

- **Windows:** click "Download R for Windows," then "base," then the download link at the top of the page. Run the installer and accept the defaults.
- **macOS:** click "Download R for macOS" and choose the installer that matches your Mac. Macs with Apple silicon (M1 and later) use the `arm64` version, and older Intel Macs use the `x86_64` version. If you aren't sure, click the Apple menu and choose "About This Mac."
- **Linux:** follow the instructions for your distribution on the CRAN page.

The course uses R 4.6. If you already have an older version, install the new one.

## Step 2: Install Positron

You won't type code into R itself. You'll work in **Positron**, an editor made by Posit, and that's what we use in class. It includes Quarto, so you can open and render the `.qmd` files for the course, and it includes the Posit Publisher extension we'll use to share homework. Install R first (step 1), then Positron:

1. Go to <https://positron.posit.co/download>, accept the license, and download the installer for your computer.
   - **Windows:** if you're offered a *user* installer and a *system* installer, choose the user installer. It doesn't need administrator rights, which matters on a UTSA-managed laptop.
   - **macOS:** open the downloaded `.dmg` file and drag Positron into your Applications folder.
2. Run the installer and accept the defaults.
3. Open Positron. The first time, it finds your R installation and starts an R session in the **Console**, the pane at the bottom of the window. If you see `R 4.6` (or similar) near the top right of the window and a `>` prompt in the Console, it's working. If it can't find R, click the interpreter button at the top right and choose your R installation, or restart Positron after checking that R installed correctly.

If you've used RStudio before, most of Positron will feel familiar: the editor, the Console, plots and help are all there, laid out a little differently.

## Step 3: Windows only, install Rtools

A few packages (`brms` in week 12, mainly) compile code in C++, and on Windows that needs [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/). Choose the version that matches your version of R and accept the defaults. On a Mac, the equivalent is the Xcode command line tools: run `xcode-select --install` in the Terminal.

## Step 4: Install the course packages

Open Positron, then copy this line into the R **Console** and press Enter:

```{r}
#| label: install-script
#| eval: false
source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/coreysparks/DEM7283/master/install_first_7283.R")
```

The script installs `pak`, a faster installer that uses prebuilt packages, and then hands it the list of packages for the semester, plus my `sparkscolors` package from GitHub. It skips anything you already have, so if it stops partway through (a dropped connection, a laptop going to sleep), run it again and it picks up where it left off. When it finishes, it prints `Done. Restart R before you start working.`

You should never run code from the internet that you haven't looked at, mine included. The script is [short](https://github.com/coreysparks/DEM7283/blob/master/install_first_7283.R).

## Step 5: Install Git and create a GitHub account

You'll keep your homework in Git and share it on GitHub, starting in week 1. If you've never used either, don't worry; [Week 1](chapters/01-intro-workflow.qmd#sec-git) explains what they are and walks through the whole setup. Before the first class, please do the first two steps from that section:

1. **Create a free GitHub account** at <https://github.com>. Use an email address you'll keep after you graduate, and pick a username you'd be happy for a future employer to see.
2. **Install Git.** On Windows, download Git for Windows from <https://git-scm.com/downloads/win> and run the installer. The defaults are fine except for two questions: for the default editor, choose Notepad instead of Vim, and for the name of the initial branch, choose to override it and type `main`. On a Mac, open the Terminal app and type `git --version`; if Git isn't there, macOS offers to install it.

We'll do the rest of the setup (connecting R to your GitHub account) together in class.

## Step 6: Get the course repository

The data and the helper functions the chapters use live in the [course repository](https://github.com/coreysparks/DEM7283). Week 1 shows you how to clone it with Git. If you want to look around before then, the green **Code** button on the repository page has a **Download ZIP** option.

## Step 7: Get a Census API key

A few of the chapters download data from the Census Bureau with `tidycensus`, which needs a free key. Request one at <https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html>; it arrives by email in a few minutes. Weeks 2 and 6 show you where to put it.

## Troubleshooting

**A package fails to install.** Read the message, then try installing that package by itself, for example `pak::pak("survey")`. On Windows, if the error mentions `make` or a compiler, check that Rtools is installed (step 3). On a Mac, if it mentions `clang` or `gfortran`, install the Xcode command line tools.

**The script can't reach GitHub.** Campus and corporate networks sometimes block it. Try again from a different network.

**Something else.** Copy the full error message and bring it to class or office hours, or email it to me. Error messages look scary, but they usually tell you exactly what went wrong.

## What gets installed

| Packages | What we use them for |
|---|---|
| `knitr`, `rmarkdown`, `quarto`, `here`, `renv`, `usethis`, `gitcreds`, `rsconnect` | Rendering documents, project paths, package versions, Git, and publishing (week 1) |
| `tidyverse`, `haven`, `ipumsr`, `tidycensus`, `tigris`, `skimr`, `scales` | Reading and managing data, Census downloads, and graphics |
| `survey`, `srvyr`, `svyVGAM` | Complex survey design (week 2 onward) |
| `modelsummary`, `marginaleffects`, `gtsummary`, `broom`, `broom.helpers`, `car`, `Hmisc` | Model tables, predicted probabilities and marginal effects |
| `VGAM`, `pscl`, `betareg` | Ordinal, multinomial, count and proportion models (weeks 3 to 6) |
| `oaxaca` | Decomposition (week 7) |
| `mice`, `mitools` | Multiple imputation (week 9) |
| `geepack`, `fixest` | GEE and fixed effects models (week 10) |
| `lme4`, `WeMix`, `brms` | Multilevel models (weeks 12 and 13) |
| `dagitty`, `ggdag`, `MatchIt`, `WeightIt`, `cobalt`, `EValue` | Causal inference (week 14) |
| `tidymodels`, `probably`, `ranger`, `xgboost`, `rpart.plot` | Machine learning (week 15) |
| `sparkscolors` | UTSA colors for graphs (from GitHub) |
